title: Monkeys Are Surprisingly Good at Shape Games
summary: Have you ever played a game where you match shapes? Monkeys can do it too — and they think about shapes a lot like we do. Scientists at Carnegie Mellon University wanted to know: are humans the only animals that understand geometry (the math of shapes)? To find out, they gave shape-matching games to preschoolers, monkeys, and adults from Bolivia and Namibia who never studied geometry in school. Everyone played on a screen. The monkeys worked for treats, like fruit cereal. The kids worked for stickers — but sometimes they said no! "You have to bargain with them," scientist Jialin Li said. One baboon named Kalamata loved the games so much he played for hours a day. The scientists watched how each group matched shapes and what mistakes they made. Then they compared those mistakes to two computer models. Here's the cool part: monkeys and humans made similar mistakes. That hints their brains might handle shapes in similar ways. "Humans are not unique in this," Li said, "but we are better." So next time you match shapes, remember — you're doing something a monkey can do too. Just maybe a little better!
why_it_matters: It shows that when you practise shapes and patterns in math class, you're using a skill that other animals share too — and scientists are still figuring out exactly how our brains do it.

background_read: The study was run by Carnegie Mellon University (a university in the United States where scientists study many different things).
The adults in the study came from Bolivia (a country in South America) and Namibia (a country in southern Africa), and had never learned geometry in school.
Baboons like Kalamata are monkeys that live in Africa, and scientists often test them because they are clever at solving puzzles.
